title: Unrolling the circle into a wave
objectives: Draw the graphs of $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$ from the point moving round the unit circle
Read values, zeros, peaks and troughs from the graphs
Use periodicity: the graphs repeat every $2\pi$

screens.prose: The point starts at angle 0, on the right of the unit circle. It turns anticlockwise once, all the way back to the start. Its height is $\sin\theta$.
screens.question: How does the height change during the turn?

options.text: Up to 1, down through 0 to −1, then back up to 0
Down from 1 to −1, then back up to 1
options.why: That is the across-distance, which starts at 1. The height starts at 0, because the point begins on the axis.

options.text: Down to −1, up through 0 to 1, then back to 0
options.why: That turns the point clockwise. Anticlockwise from the right, the point rises first.

options.text: Up to 1 and back to 0, twice
options.why: You measured distance from the axis without its sign. Below the axis the height is negative, down to −1.

hints.text: Picture the point at the top, the left, the bottom and back at the start.
The height is the vertical segment from the axis to the point.
Quarter turns: top (height 1), left (0), bottom (−1), start (0).

feedback.correct: Up, down through zero, and back: one full wave.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the height at each quarter turn.

explain.text: At the quarter turns the height is 0, 1, 0, −1 and 0 again. Between them it changes smoothly. Plotting those heights against the angle draws a wave, as we will see next.

screens.prose: The circle sits on the left. Move the slider to turn the point. Its height is carried across by the dashed line and plotted above the angle $x$.
screens.question: At which angle does the curve reach its lowest point?

options.why: At $\pi$ the point is at the far left of the circle, height 0. The lowest point is a quarter turn later.
At $2\pi$ the point is back at the start, height 0.

hints.text: Watch the point on the circle. When is it at the very bottom?

feedback.correct: Three quarters of a turn puts the point at the bottom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the point on the circle is at the bottom, and read the angle.

explain.text: At $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ the point is at the bottom of the circle, height −1. The curve's lowest point is directly across from it. Each point of the curve is a height of the circle point, plotted above its angle.

screens.prose: The curve you drew is the **graph of sine**, $y = \sin x$, with $x$ the angle in radians. One full turn draws one full wave. The length of one wave, $2\pi$, is its **period**.
screens.question: Tap every marked point where $\sin x = 0$.

hints.text: Where is the point on the circle level with the centre?
The curve is at height 0 where it meets the horizontal axis.
The point is on the horizontal axis at the start, after a half turn and after a full turn.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find every place where the curve meets the horizontal axis, ends included.

byKey.inside: You found $\pi$. The two ends, 0 and $2\pi$, are on the axis too: the point starts and finishes there.
byKey.peaks: Those are the highest and lowest points, where $\sin x$ is 1 and −1.
byKey.z1: At $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ the curve is at its top, $\sin x = 1$.
byKey.z3: At $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ the curve is at its bottom, $\sin x = -1$.

explain.text: The point is on the horizontal axis at 0, $\pi$ and $2\pi$, so $\sin x = 0$ there. The ends count: $2\pi$ is the same point as 0. The wave then starts again.

screens.prose: Now plot the across-distance instead of the height. At angle 0 the point is at $(1, 0)$, so $\cos 0 = 1$.
screens.question: Drag the five points to sketch $y = \cos x$ from 0 to $2\pi$.

hints.text: Where is the point at each quarter turn? Read its across-distance.
The five points sit at 0, $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$, $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ and $2\pi$.
Right, top, left, bottom, right: across-distances 1, 0, −1, 0, 1.

feedback.correct: Cosine starts at its peak, falls to −1 at $\pi$, and climbs back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the across-distance at each quarter turn.

byKey.sine: You drew the height, which is sine. Cosine is the across-distance, and it starts at 1.
byKey.flipped: Your curve is upside down. At angle 0 the point is one unit to the right, so $\cos 0 = 1$, not −1.

explain.text: Right, top, left, bottom, right gives 1, 0, −1, 0, 1. Joining them smoothly draws $y = \cos x$. It is the same wave shape as sine, starting at its peak.

screens.prose: Keep turning past $2\pi$. The graph carries on to the right. Here are two full turns, and an angle of $\tfrac{13\pi}{6}$ is marked.
screens.question: What is $\sin\tfrac{13\pi}{6}$?

hints.text: How much more than one full turn is $\tfrac{13\pi}{6}$?
$\tfrac{13\pi}{6} = 2\pi + \tfrac{\pi}{6}$.
After a full turn the point is back where it started, so it is at $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$, which is 30°. Use $\sin 30^\circ$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take away a full turn first.

byKey.neg: The point is just past the start of its second turn, above the axis. The height is positive.
byKey.zero: Zero is at $2\pi$ itself. $\tfrac{13\pi}{6}$ is $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ further on.
byKey.cos: That is $\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6}$, the across-distance. Sine is the height.

explain.text: Taking away $2\pi$ leaves $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$, which is 30°, so the height is 0.5. The second wave copies the first, shifted right by $2\pi$. A function that repeats like this is **periodic**.

screens.prose: Sine and cosine look alike. The solid wave is $y = \sin(x + h)$; the slider changes $h$ and slides it left. The dashed wave is $y = \cos x$.
screens.question: Set $h$ so the solid wave lies on the dashed one.

hints.text: Where does each wave have its first peak?
Sine peaks at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Cosine peaks at 0.
Slide sine left by the gap between the peaks: $\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Line up the peaks of the two waves.

byKey.pi: A shift of $\pi$ turns the wave upside down: peaks land on troughs. Half of that is enough.
byKey.one: You moved it by about 1. The peaks are $\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$ apart.

explain.text: Sine peaks a quarter turn after cosine. Sliding it left by $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ lines the waves up exactly. So $\cos x = \sin(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2})$: one wave, started at different points.

screens.prose: The point on the circle is at angle 2 radians. On the circle, its across-distance is $\cos 2 \approx -0.42$. We want its partner on the graph of $y = \sin x$.
screens.question: What is the horizontal coordinate of the partner point on the graph?

options.why: You carried the circle's across-distance over to the graph. On the graph, the horizontal axis is the angle itself.
The height is the partner's vertical coordinate. Across the graph we plot the angle.

hints.text: What does the horizontal axis of the graph count?
The axis is labelled angle $x$ in radians.
The partner sits above the angle, $x = 2$, at the circle point's height, $\sin 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what the graph's horizontal axis measures.

byKey.cos: You took $x$ on the graph to be the point's across-distance. The circle's $x$-coordinate is $\cos$ of the angle; the graph's $x$ is the angle.

explain.text: On the circle, $x$ and $y$ are the point's coordinates, $(\cos 2, \sin 2)$. On the graph, $x$ is the angle and $y$ is the height, giving $(2, \sin 2)$. The same letter $x$ means two different things.

screens.prose: Both graphs repeat every full turn, and both stay between −1 and 1, the radius. In symbols: $$\sin(x + 2\pi) = \sin x, \quad \cos(x + 2\pi) = \cos x, \quad -1 \le \sin x \le 1.$$
screens.question: Which value can $\sin x$ never take?

options.why: $\sin x = -1$ at $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, the bottom of the circle.
Large angles just go round again. $\sin \tfrac{13\pi}{6} = 0.5$.

hints.text: How high can a point on a circle of radius 1 be?
The height is never more than the radius, 1, and never less than −1.

feedback.correct: A height on the unit circle never passes 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of the highest and lowest points of the unit circle.

explain.text: The point never rises above 1 or falls below −1. So $\sin x$ can never be 1.2, whatever the angle. Every value from −1 to 1 comes round again every $2\pi$.

screens.prose: You saw the second wave copy the first. Now show why it must, for any angle $x$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Turning by $x + 2\pi$ means turning by $x$, then one more full turn
A full turn of $2\pi$ brings the point back to where it was
So the points at $x + 2\pi$ and at $x$ are the same point, with the same coordinates
So $\sin(x + 2\pi) = \sin x$ and $\cos(x + 2\pi) = \cos x$, reading the height and the across-distance

hints.text: Split the turn $x + 2\pi$ into two parts.
What does the full turn do to the point?
Split the turn, undo the full turn, compare the points, then read off sine and cosine.

feedback.correct: A full turn changes nothing, so the values repeat.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by splitting the turn into $x$ and a full turn.

byKey.d4: Read off the coordinates last, once you know the two points are the same.
byKey.d3: You need the effect of the full turn before you can say the points match.

explain.text: Splitting the turn and undoing the full turn shows the two points coincide. Equal points have equal coordinates, so both functions repeat. Their period is $2\pi$.

screens.prose: A retailer models monthly demand, in thousands of units, as $D = 100 + 30\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi m}{6}\right)$. Here $m$ counts months from the start of January, so $m = 12$ is a full turn.

params.xLabel: months from the start of January

screens.question: How many months after the start of January is demand lowest?

hints.text: Sine is lowest at a particular angle. Which one?
The lowest point of $\sin$ is at the angle $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$.
Solve $\tfrac{\pi m}{6} = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$: $m = 9$.

feedback.correct: Nine months in, at the start of October.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the month whose angle $\tfrac{\pi m}{6}$ is $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

byKey.half: At $m = 6$ the angle is $\pi$: demand is back at its average, 100, and still falling.
byKey.peak: At $m = 3$ the angle is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. That is the busiest month, not the quietest.
byKey.radians: 4.71 is the angle $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ in radians. Turn it back into months: $m = \tfrac{6}{\pi} \times 4.71 = 9$.

explain.text: Demand is lowest when the sine is −1, at angle $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$. That needs $\tfrac{\pi m}{6} = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so $m = 9$, with demand $100 - 30 = 70$ thousand. The cycle repeats every 12 months.

ideas: Plot the point's height against its angle and you get $y = \sin x$; plot its across-distance and you get $y = \cos x$.
Both graphs repeat every full turn: the period is $2\pi$, and both stay between −1 and 1.
Cosine is sine slid left by a quarter turn: $\cos x = \sin(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2})$.

formula.name: Periodicity
formula.note: The same holds for cosine. Zeros of sine: $0, \pi, 2\pi, \ldots$

summary.trap: On the graph, $x$ is the angle, not the point's across-distance. The circle point $(\cos x, \sin x)$ becomes the graph point $(x, \sin x)$.

quiz.prose: The graph of $y = \sin x$ repeats itself.
quiz.question: What is its period, with $x$ in radians?

options.why: After $\pi$ the wave has gone up and come back to 0, but it then goes negative. It repeats only after $2\pi$.
360 is a full turn in degrees. With $x$ in radians, a full turn is $2\pi$.
1 is the height of the peak, not the length of a wave.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How far must $x$ go before the point is back where it started?

explain.text: The wave repeats when the point completes a turn. In radians a turn is $2\pi$. So the period of $y = \sin x$ is $2\pi \approx 6.28$.

quiz.prose: Read from the graph of $y = \cos x$.
quiz.question: What is $\cos\pi$?

options.why: That is $\sin\pi$. Cosine is at its lowest at $\pi$.
Cosine is 1 at 0 and at $2\pi$. Halfway between, it is at the bottom.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where is the point after a half turn?

explain.text: After a half turn the point is at $(-1, 0)$. Its across-distance is −1. So the cosine graph has its trough at $x = \pi$.

quiz.prose: Use the fact that sine repeats.
quiz.question: What is $\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take away a full turn of $2\pi$ first.

byKey.zero: $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$ is not a whole number of half turns. Take away $2\pi$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is left.
byKey.neg: −1 is at $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$. After taking away $2\pi$, we are at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, the top.

explain.text: $\tfrac{5\pi}{2} = 2\pi + \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. The full turn changes nothing, so the point is at the top. The height is 1.

quiz.question: Which graph is at its highest when $x = 0$?

options.why: Sine starts at 0 and rises. Its peak is at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
At $x = 0$ the point is at $(1, 0)$: across-distance 1, height 0. Only one starts at its peak.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where is the point at angle 0?

explain.text: At angle 0 the point is at $(1, 0)$. So $\cos 0 = 1$, the highest cosine can be, while $\sin 0 = 0$. Cosine is sine started a quarter turn early.
